Quantifying and Avoiding Unfair Qualification Labour in Crowdsourcing

paper.acl.2021.acl-short.44

Prepared 15 Nov 2026 · Evidence snapshot 12 Nov 2026 · Report research-2026-11-12.1 · Evidence research-2026-11-11.candidate.1

Evidence & scope

Substantive bounded primary methods/results/limitations source review is documented at ACL-Anthology-2021.acl-short.44-captured-2026-11-10. Qualification-cell and task-dependent calibration content establishes crowdsourcing recruitment/evaluation relevance. Estimated forum labor and small cells remain bounded rather than representative population measurements. Original author/source-verifier/adversarial receipts bind every exact approved fact; unread pages, unreplicated experiments and source conflicts remain recorded in the pinned dossier. This admission is for one logical paper work only.

Approved findings

Approved evidence · As of 10 Nov 2026

Qualification effects were task dependent, and workers self-selected by returning HITs; the paper recommends calibrating the lowest suitable threshold and warns that higher approval-percentage requirements can increase vulnerability to unfair rejection.

Approved evidence · As of 10 Nov 2026

The study compared worker performance across 15 combinations of approved-HIT counts and approval percentages on coreference and sentiment tasks, restricting recruitment to U.S.-based MTurk workers.

Approved evidence · As of 10 Nov 2026

Coreference used a 244-word OntoNotes document with parsed noun phrases; sentiment followed Stanford Sentiment Treebank instructions. The authors targeted $12 per hour and reported worker-reported hourly rates separately.

Approved evidence · As of 10 Nov 2026

In the follow-up coreference condition requiring 99–100% approval and 1, 000+ approved HITs, 60 of 92 workers scored at least 80 F-score; the task-level qualification patterns differed between coreference and sentiment.
